w015.note: Asklepios is a healing god of myth and cult; there is no datable medical advance.

w016.note: Hesiod's Pandora myth explains the origin of disease; it is not a medical advance.

w017.note: Homeric epic describes wound care and healing drugs as literature; there is no datable event.

w022.note: Empedocles' theory of four elements is philosophy; its medical use, humoral theory, has no single datable event.

w027.note: A line in a Sophocles tragedy, not a medical event.

w042.note: Pliny's Natural History is a general encyclopedia whose medical books compile earlier knowledge.

w049.note: A compilation of remedies from vegetables and fruit, with no new advance.

w050.note: A lost book on urine, known only from later references.

w056.note: A Latin adaptation of the Greek physician Soranus, not a new advance.

w057.note: A Latin handbook compiled from Greek sources.

w058.note: 'Monastic medicine' is a broad tradition, not a datable event.

w061.note: An encyclopedia compiling earlier Greek medicine.

w069.note: A Byzantine summary of earlier medicine.

w083.note: General writings that include medicine, without a specific advance.

w085.note: Translation of Arabic medical works into Greek; the translation movement is represented by Hunayn ibn Ishaq.

w098.note: 'Scholastic medicine' is a broad movement, not a datable event.

w107.note: A late Byzantine compendium of earlier knowledge.

w111.note: A philosophical work reconciling medicine and philosophy, not a medical advance.

w124.note: Clowes's surgical writings are not tied to a specific advance; the surgeon's chest belongs with John Woodall (w132).

w004.note: The date of 3000 BCE has no historical basis. The earliest Ayurvedic texts, the compendia of Charaka and Sushruta, date from the last centuries BCE and are covered separately.

w005.note: Imhotep's reputation as a physician comes from his deification more than 2,000 years after he lived; there is no contemporary evidence that he practised medicine.

w020.note: Bian Que is a semi-legendary figure; the attributions of acupuncture and pulse diagnosis come from much later writings.

w064.note: The story that Nestorian institutions at Gondishapur became the model for Islamic hospitals is not supported by current scholarship.

w067.note: Aaron's Pandects survive only in fragments quoted by later writers, so the claimed first mention of smallpox and measles cannot be verified. Al-Razi's distinction of the two diseases is in the atlas.

w079.note: The claim that Donnolo founded the school of Salerno is a legend; his Hebrew pharmacological writing is not tied to a specific advance.

w018.note: The Hippocratic tradition associated with Cos is represented by the Sacred Disease entry; the idea of rival medical schools at Cnidos and Cos is largely a later construction.

w052.note: Julian's order for xenones is described in the entry on Basil's Basileias.

w129.note: Earlier observations of the venous valves, such as Amato Lusitano's, are noted in the Fabrici entry.
